subsystems.name: Collector telescope
subsystems.role: a modest telescope, of order a metre, gathers the light that solar gravity has bent into a thin ring around the Sun.
parts: coronagraph to suppress the Sun's glare

subsystems.name: Spacecraft bus and pointing
subsystems.role: holds the telescope fixed on the Sun for days at a time while the whole spacecraft drifts to scan the ring.

subsystems.name: Propulsion
subsystems.role: supplies the very large velocity change needed to leave the inner solar system fast.
parts: solar sail or chemical stage for a close solar flyby

subsystems.name: Power
subsystems.role: runs instruments and heaters for decades where sunlight is negligible.
parts: radioisotope thermoelectric generator or small fission reactor

subsystems.name: Communications
subsystems.role: sends images back across hundreds of astronomical units.
parts: large high-gain antenna or laser terminal

subsystems.name: Ground image processing
subsystems.role: inverts the ring-shaped raw data into a picture of a planet's surface.

buildSteps.title: Pick the target and fix the geometry
buildSteps.detail: Choose an exoplanet system and calculate exactly where along the focal line the spacecraft must sit to receive its light.

buildSteps.title: Design the optics around the ring
buildSteps.detail: The telescope must reject the Sun's overwhelming glare while keeping the faint planet signal, so the coronagraph and stray-light baffling dominate the design.

buildSteps.title: Build and test the payload
buildSteps.detail: Mirror, coronagraph and detector are assembled and tested in vacuum on the ground and, ideally, demonstrated in Earth orbit first.

buildSteps.title: Integrate the spacecraft
buildSteps.detail: Power source, antenna, propulsion and autonomous navigation are stacked and balanced around the telescope's needs.

buildSteps.title: Launch and boost
buildSteps.detail: After launch, the spacecraft performs a close solar flyby or unfurls a large solar sail to gain the extreme speed required.

buildSteps.title: Cruise for decades
buildSteps.detail: The craft coasts outward, navigating by radio ranging and optical tracking so its position relative to the focal line stays known.

buildSteps.title: Cross the focal region
buildSteps.detail: At roughly 550 AU and beyond, it turns the telescope back toward the Sun and scans slowly across the Einstein ring, integrating for hours to days per position.

buildSteps.title: Reconstruct the image
buildSteps.detail: The ring data are transmitted home and computationally unwrapped into a resolved view of the planet.

prerequisites.why: the farthest spacecraft, Voyager 1, is still only about a third of that distance after nearly 50 years of flight.
starlight must be suppressed by many orders of magnitude to see a planet beside the Sun.
image quality depends on knowing the spacecraft's offset from the focal line to a tiny fraction of the ring's radius.
radioisotope generators already run spacecraft for decades, though with slowly falling output.
the raw signal is a smeared annulus, not a picture, and must be mathematically inverted.

pathway.milestone: concept studies funded through NASA's Innovative Advanced Concepts programme, plus advances in coronagraphs on ground and space telescopes
pathway.unlocks: a credible mission architecture and target list.

pathway.milestone: a precursor probe to tens or hundreds of AU demonstrating sail or flyby propulsion, autonomous navigation and optical communication
pathway.unlocks: the engineering confidence to commit to a 25-year cruise.

pathway.milestone: the first dedicated lens mission parked in the focal region and returning a resolved image of a nearby exoplanet
pathway.unlocks: direct surface and atmosphere mapping of worlds we currently see only as dots.

pathway.milestone: several spacecraft spread along the focal line, each observing different systems
pathway.unlocks: a genuine imaging observatory for exoplanets within a few tens of light years.
